extracted.intended_audience: university faculty, students, and others involved in forming or evaluating English Catholic literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for what constitutes great literature generally and specifically for the project of creating a Catholic literature in English; aimed at clarifying realistic aims and the kinds of works/craftsmanship to encourage in a Catholic university context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic aim: expression adequate to subject and appropriate to speaker
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist ... has his great or rich visions before him, and his only aim is to bring out what he thinks or what he feels in a way adequate to the thing spoken of, and appropriate to the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with the 'mere dealer in words' who embellishes anything to order; the true literary artist prioritises fidelity to his subject-matter and to his own voice rather than verbal ornament for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translatability is not a test of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: To be capable of easy translation is no test of the excellence of a composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Languages are not all alike; great authors mould their native tongues and create idiosyncratic expressions which often cannot be reproduced in another language. Analogies: it is absurd to disparage Beethoven because his piano music cannot be played on the hurdy-gurdy; similarly inability to translate fully into another tongue does not diminish genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery and personal presence in native language
rubrics_metrics.description: A great author takes his native language, masters it, partly throws himself into it, partly moulds and adapts it, and pours out his multitude of ideas through the variously ramified and delicately minute channels of expression which he has found or framed:—does it follow that this his personal presence ... can forthwith be transferred to every other language?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's personal linguistic 'presence' is integral to excellence; attempts to judge authors solely by how their work reads in translation ignore this essential fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each art/language has its own subject-matter and capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the Fine Arts has its own subject-matter; from the nature of the case you can do in one what you cannot do in another ... you can do in oils what you cannot do in fresco.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to languages: genius may achieve in Greek what it cannot in Latin; inability to reproduce effects across arts or languages is natural and does not indicate defect. Do not demand cross-medium or cross-language equivalence as a standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Literature (personal) and Science (objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature is of a personal character; Science treats of what is universal and eternal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portions of Scripture that 'rise into the region of pure and mere inspiration' resemble Science (objective enunciation) and are easier to translate; by contrast, literary, personal writings (e.g., St. Paul's epistles) have the complexity of literature and demand the same considerations as other great authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture contains elaborate literary workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture not elaborate! Scripture not ornamented in diction, and musical in cadence!—Why, consider the Epistle to the Hebrews ... the book of Job ... the Psalter—are there no ornaments, no rhythm, no studied cadences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the assumption that sacred texts are necessarily simple or easily paraphrased; recognising the literary art in Scripture explains why faithful and pure translation is difficult and why good translators are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Literature: expression of thought in language
rubrics_metrics.description: By Letters or Literature is meant the expression of thought in language, where by 'thought' I mean the ideas, feelings, views, reasonings, and other operations of the human mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Art of Letters is the method by which a speaker or writer brings out in words, worthy of his subject, and sufficient for his audience or readers, the thoughts which impress him. Evaluate works by how well they express those thoughts in fitting language for their audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance plus facility of expression (two-fold Logos)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great author ... is one who has something to say and knows how to say it. ... I ascribe to him, as his characteristic gift, in a large sense the faculty of Expression. He is master of the two-fold Logos, the thought and the word, distinct, but inseparable from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse rhetorical copia (mere store of phrases) with genuine authorship. Both idea (content) and its expression must be judged; either without the other is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness, precision, and economy of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: He always has the right word for the right idea, and never a word too much. If he is brief, it is because few words suffice; when he is lavish of them, still each word has its mark, and aids, not embarrasses, the vigorous march of his elocution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction for suitability to idea and to the work's rhythm; verbosity that does not add meaning is a fault, while measured ornament can be appropriate when each word contributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, analytic richness, consistency, and lucidity
rubrics_metrics.description: He writes passionately, because he feels keenly; forcibly, because he conceives vividly; he sees too clearly to be vague; he is too serious to be otiose; he can analyze his subject, and therefore he is rich; he embraces it as a whole and in its parts, and therefore he is consistent; he has a firm hold of it, and therefore he is luminous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A great work combines emotional force with intellectual clarity and structural coherence; judge works by these interrelated qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament and emotion should arise naturally from imagination and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: When his imagination wells up, it overflows in ornament; when his heart is touched, it thrills along his verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornamentation is appropriate when it is the natural overflow of imagination or feeling; contrived or gratuitous ornament is to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catholic Literature ≠ religious literature; include all subjects treated as a Catholic would treat them
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'Catholic Literature' is not to be understood a literature which treats exclusively or primarily of Catholic matters ... but it includes all subjects of literature whatever, treated as a Catholic would treat them, and as he only can treat them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting a Catholic literature, do not restrict to theological works; encourage works across genres where the author's Catholic perspective informs treatment, but avoid equating the project with merely creating a library of religious texts or a seminary curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay writers should not be compelled into polemical/seminary roles
rubrics_metrics.description: A lecturer or writer so employed must not be entangling himself in a semi-clerical occupation ... Men think that he cannot give a lecture on Comparative Anatomy without being bound to digress into the Argument from Final Causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not presume that Catholic-affiliated literary activity requires polemical or clerical digressions; authors should be free to treat secular subjects without forced theological applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific works are universal; need not be 'Catholicized' to be fit for use
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards mathematics, chemistry, astronomy, and similar subjects, one man will not, on the score of his religion, treat of them better than another ... There is no crying demand, no imperative necessity, for our acquisition of a Catholic Euclid or a Catholic Newton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In building a Catholic university library or curriculum, prioritize literature and matters where religious perspective importantly changes treatment; use scientific works by non-Catholics where their science is sound, while remaining cautious about authors' extraneous opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical realism about the formation of a national 'Catholic' literature
rubrics_metrics.description: A Literature, when it is formed, is a national and historical fact ... We cannot write a new Milton or a new Gibbon; we cannot expurgate what needs to be exorcised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect a university initiative to instantaneously create a national classical literature. Recognize the existing canon and the historical formation of national literatures; set feasible aims and avoid impossible schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept and use non-Catholic authoritative works within their proper bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: We allow our Catholic student to use them, so far as he can surprise them ... in their formal treatises, and can keep them close prisoners there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to adopt scientific or critical works by non-Catholics for instruction, provided their influence is confined to their technical content; beware of adopting authors wholesale when their personal opinions would be objectionable in a formative educational context.
